answer: The place I would like to describe is my university campus, where I spent some of the most [[formative]] years of my life. It was a large, leafy campus on the outskirts of the city, with old buildings, a big central field and plenty of open green space. I studied there for four years, doing a BBA with a focus on management, and I graduated a few years ago. What I loved was how [[vibrant]] the atmosphere was; there was always something happening, from lectures and presentations to club activities and cultural programmes. I joined the debating club, which did wonders for my confidence and my English. The library in particular became a second home, a wonderfully [[studious]] environment that made it easy to focus, especially before exams. Beyond the academics, the campus was where I made lifelong friendships and grew as a person, partly because it was my first time living away from my family. Looking back, those years were genuinely [[pivotal]] in shaping who I am today, and even the skills I use at work now, like advising students and giving presentations, started there. There was a real sense of community, and everyone seemed to be striving towards something together. I still remember the long conversations over cheap tea at the canteen after classes. Honestly, I feel a strong sense of [[nostalgia]] whenever I think about it. I think a good campus offers far more than an education, and mine certainly did.

followUps.q: Do you still visit your university?
followUps.answer: Only occasionally, when I have work nearby or there is an alumni event. It always feels a little strange, because the faces are all new, but walking across the field still brings back lots of memories.

followUps.q: What did you like least about studying there?
followUps.answer: Probably the stressful exam periods, when the library was so full you could hardly find a seat, and missing home cooking. Still, those challenges were part of the experience, and they taught me independence.
